idiom_name: continuity class owning std::map<system_clock::time_point, Version> with upper_bound as-of lookup
implementation_notes: The continuity is an ordinary class owning a std::map keyed by a std::chrono time point whose values are immutable Version objects: as-of is one std::map::upper_bound() call stepped back one element and current is the last entry, so the temporal collection collapses into the ordered container and no search code remains. A new version is built as a value copy of the one in force (Version working = current(); working.setFee(...)) and inserted at its effective date, which keeps every published state frozen while retroactive and future-dated amendments stay ordinary inserts. Choose this node-based form when history is sparse; the flat-vector variant wins when the whole history is traversed repeatedly (reports, period enumeration).
pitfalls: Boundary error: the version in force is the greatest key <= date, i.e. upper_bound() stepped back; lower_bound() silently returns the next version when the query date is exactly an effective date.
A member accessor that hands out Terms& lets callers mutate published history; return const& or values and always edit a copy (working copy, then insert).
std::map allocates a node per version and has poor cache locality; recording many versions for one object should use the flat-vector variant or a coarser effective-date granularity.

Changing the key granularity is a semantic change: converting timestamps to day keys (std::chrono::floor<days>) can move an effective moment into the previous version, so the floor/ceil rule must be explicit and shared.

variants.name: Sorted value vector with std::upper_bound (contiguous, scan-friendly)
variants.implementation_notes: Store the history as one contiguous ascending vector of (effective, Version) pairs: as-of is std::upper_bound over the whole vector (one comparison per probe, cache-friendly), current is back(), and period enumeration is a plain loop - the form reports, deltas and proration want. The price is insertion: a retroactive amendment memmoves the tail and invalidates every iterator, pointer and reference into the vector, so the continuity must publish snapshots by value (or re-fetch after mutating) and should reserve capacity for the expected version count. Prefer it over the map variant when reads dominate writes and whole-history scans are common.
pitfalls: Insertion is O(n) and invalidates every pointer, reference and iterator into the vector - never hold &Version across an amendment.
Contiguous storage rewards compact version types; string-heavy snapshots reallocate large blocks per insert, which is the case the map variant handles better.
The vector must stay ascending by effective date: a blind push_back of a retroactive amendment breaks std::upper_bound's precondition and yields a wrong version without any error.

variants.name: C++20 calendar dates as history keys (sys_days / year_month_day)
variants.idiom_name: std::chrono::sys_days keys with std::chrono::year_month_day at the API edge
variants.implementation_notes: C++20's calendar types make the effective date a calendar fact instead of an instant: key the history by std::chrono::sys_days (or take std::chrono::year_month_day in the API) so a version is 'in force from 2024-02-01' rather than 'from an arbitrary timestamp', and use calendar arithmetic (ymd + std::chrono::months{3}, normalization through sys_days) for proration and period enumeration. As-of stays a transparent-comparator map lookup. Two traps: local_days and sys_days share a representation but not a meaning, and calendar support is not uniform across standard libraries, so the build must actually require C++20.
pitfalls: local_days and sys_days have the same underlying representation but different meaning; building keys from local_days puts the whole history in a timezone-dependent frame.
year_month_day{2024y/February/30d} is constructible but invalid: converting it to sys_days normalizes to March 1 instead of rejecting the date, quietly shifting an effective date.
Day keys discard the time of day, so two amendments on the same day collapse to one entry unless the model defines a within-day tie-break rule.
